```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

A cohort usually has an enormous number of maximum sets, all of the same size. Choosing one
of them is arbitrary, and the individuals analysed, and therefore the results of the
analysis, depend on that choice. This vignette shows how RedKinNet quantifies this
uncertainty on the example cohort, with the network built as in *Get started with
RedKinNet*.

```{r}
library(RedKinNet)
kin <- rkn_example$kinship
covariates <- rkn_example$samples
chk <- rkn_check_samples(kin, threshold = "third", samples = covariates$id)
g <- rkn_graph_from_kinship(kin, threshold = "third", samples = covariates$id,
                            exclude = chk$contamination$id, covariates = covariates,
                            check = FALSE)
```

## How many maximum sets

A uniform selection counts the maximum sets of every family exactly. The number for the
whole network is the product of the numbers of the families.

```{r}
sel <- rkn_select_random(g, uniform = TRUE, seed = 1)
sel
fs <- sel$family_summary
head(fs[order(-fs$n_max_sets), c("family_id", "family_size", "n_kept", "n_max_sets")])
```

## Inclusion probabilities

The inclusion probability of an individual is the proportion of the maximum sets that
contain it, which is its probability of being selected by a uniform draw. Individuals with
probability 1 are selected in every maximum set, those with probability 0 in none; only the
others are actually chosen.

```{r}
p <- sel$node_diagnostics$inclusion_probability
table(cut(p, c(-0.01, 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.99, 1),
          labels = c("0", "(0, 0.25]", "(0.25, 0.5]", "(0.5, 0.75]", "(0.75, 1)", "1")))
```

Two independent uniform draws differ, on average, in the sum of `p * (1 - p)` selected
individuals, the figure reported by `print()`.

```{r}
sum(p * (1 - p))
```

## How much a result can change

Repeating the uniform draw with different seeds shows how much a statistic computed on the
selected individuals varies across equally valid selections. Here the statistics are the
proportion of women and the mean age; in a real study they would be the results of the
downstream analysis. Each seed gives an independent draw.

```{r}
draws <- data.frame(seed = 1:50, women = NA_real_, mean_age = NA_real_)
for (s in draws$seed) {
  kept <- rkn_select_random(g, uniform = TRUE, seed = s, diagnostics = FALSE)$kept
  i <- match(kept, covariates$id)
  draws$women[s] <- mean(covariates$sex[i] == "F", na.rm = TRUE)
  draws$mean_age[s] <- mean(covariates$age[i], na.rm = TRUE)
}
summary(draws[, c("women", "mean_age")])
```

The spread of these values is part of the uncertainty of any result obtained on one
selection. Reporting the seed, the number of maximum sets and the average difference between
draws makes the selection reproducible and its arbitrariness visible; repeating the analysis
over several draws shows whether a conclusion depends on it.

## Why uniform

The default selection of `rkn_select_random()` resolves larger families by structural rules,
which never choose some of their maximum sets. On a chain of six relatives, for instance,
there are four maximum sets, and the rules choose only between the two of alternate
relatives. A uniform draw gives every maximum set the same chance, so that the inclusion
probabilities above describe the selection exactly.

```{r}
chain <- igraph::make_graph(~ A - B - C - D - E - F)
rules <- character(200)
uniform <- character(200)
for (s in 1:200) {
  rules[s] <- paste(sort(rkn_select_random(chain, seed = s, diagnostics = FALSE)$kept), collapse = "")
  uniform[s] <- paste(sort(rkn_select_random(chain, uniform = TRUE, seed = s, diagnostics = FALSE)$kept),
                      collapse = "")
}
table(rules)
table(uniform)
```
